To burn Troy was to burn the whole world altogether." 
There is something profoundly devastating in that line. It carries an agony so vivid, a sorrow so immense, that it seems to contain the weight of an entire civilization's destruction. Behind the triumph that history celebrates lies a man burdened by the horrors he himself helped unleash. No one asked what it cost him. No one cared to know what he had endured, what parts of his soul had been left in ashes along with the city. The victors rejoiced, intoxicated by glory, while the scars borne by those who carried out that victory remained unseen and unspoken. 
These few words capture the emotional heart of the scene, the culmination of grief, guilt, loss, and disillusionment. They transcend the narrative itself and become something deeply philosophical. Great stories do not merely entertain; they challenge our assumptions, correct our understanding, mourn the forgotten, glorify the overlooked, and sometimes expose the darkness hidden within those we have long called heroes. They compel us to reconsider the moral certainty of victory and the true cost of conquest. 
Indeed, to burn Troy was not simply to destroy a city; it was to destroy a world. And in doing so, perhaps, a part of oneself as well.

That line reminded me of Nolan’s last film Oppenheimer when he realizes he’s changed humanity forever by helping introduce the atomic bomb to the world. With immense victory comes an extreme cost and most aren’t able to handle the consequences of their actions.

What if the Odysseus you knew lost his way? What if...one night, in a strange city, he saw things that made him think the home he knew couldn't possibly be there anymore. What if…when he left the belly of the horse, and opened the gates of Troy, he saw ten years of rage pour into that city in one night?

We left them a gift, an offering of peace, that they took into their home. We violated all that's ever sacred between people. It turned a fight into a hunt.

To burn the walls of Troy was to burn the world-entire. Including his home.

What if he knew, that very night, as he walked through fires, anarchy, and pain—and in a daze of sweaty celebrations that follow—what if he knew exactly what he'd done?

Penelope: What all of you had done?

One man's idea. One man's trick to break Zeus's law forever. We lived in a world of palaces and trade, language, blind to its beauty, until we broke it.

Penelope: You are the people from the sea.

Yes, my queen. The breaking of Zeus's law, spreading like plague. Our age of bronze is collapsing, and maybe he couldn't bear to see the ruins of what he'd done. Anywhere. Least of all, his home.
